camaraderie

/kah-muh-RAH-duh-ree/ - the stress falls on RAH · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Camaraderie means warm friendship and trust among a group.

A season of muddy vans and cold pizza gave the rowing team a camaraderie the new coach could feel from the dock.

Example

The touring company played forty towns in fifty nights, hauling the same set up the same narrow stairs. By the last week they had a language of nods and eyebrow flicks, and the camaraderie backstage was thicker than any plot on stage.

Camaraderie is friendship's group form — the warm, joking trust that grows when people share work, risk, or long hours. One person cannot have it; it lives between the members of a crew.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

fellowship: Fellowship is the warm feeling of belonging to a community — a congregation, a club, a scholarly society — often gathered around a shared belief. Camaraderie is earned differently: not by believing together but by working together, through the long hours a crew puts in side by side.

solidarity: Solidarity is standing together behind a cause — a unity of purpose that can bind complete strangers. Camaraderie cannot be had with strangers: it is the warm, joking trust of people who have shared work, risk, or long hours, and it has to be earned in company.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

rivalry: members competing against one another instead of pulling together

estrangement: the bond gone cold — people once close, now distant

Where it sits · how deep the group's bond runs

familiarity → camaraderie → brotherhood

familiarity vs. camaraderie: Familiarity is much weaker than camaraderie — being familiar only means the faces and habits are known, while camaraderie adds the warmth a group earns by pulling through shared work together.

brotherhood vs. camaraderie: Brotherhood goes further than camaraderie — the crew's warmth hardened into something lifelong, closer to family than to friendship.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — camarad-: comrade — literally a chamber-mate, from Latin camera, 'room'

Suffix — -erie: French: the state or quality of

Put it together: Camarad- (comrade, a chamber-mate) + -erie (the state of) = the bond of those who share a room. Latin camera, 'a room,' became Spanish camarada — soldiers who slept in the same quarters — and French carried it on to camaraderie. The word never forgot the barracks: it still means the warmth of people packed into shared space and shared work.

Use the root in a new word: chamber: The judge read the motion in her chamber before returning to the bench.

Strength Check

Word Choice

warm / neutral

Camaraderie names what a group earns together — the joking trust of a crew, a cast, a shift. It is not for two people: for an easy one-to-one understanding, this unit gives you rapport, and for strangers united behind a cause, solidarity. Reach for camaraderie when shared work has made a whole group warm.
